identification.bodyShape: A slender-bodied grouper in the same genus as gag, with a more concave head profile than gag and pronounced elongation of the soft dorsal and anal fin rays in mature fish.
identificationTraits: Pronounced anal and soft dorsal fin-ray extensions in mature specimens, producing elongated caudal-fin lobes.
Head profile is more concave than gag's.
Tan-to-grayish-brown body covered with sharply defined, well-separated dark or reddish-brown spots roughly 1/8 in across, sometimes grouped into rosettes.
Yellow coloration is limited to the corners of the mouth - the key field distinction from the closely related yellowmouth grouper, which shows yellow both inside and at the corners of the mouth.
identification.coloration: Tan to grayish-brown or light gray body with well-separated dark or reddish-brown spots, sometimes clustered into rosette patterns.
identification.adultAppearance: A slender, spotted grouper with a concave head profile and elongated soft dorsal/anal/caudal fin-ray tips in mature fish.
identification.sexualDimorphism: Protogynous hermaphrodite - individuals transition from female to male as they age. Sources describe the elongated fin-ray tips as a trait of 'mature specimens' generally, without confirming it is sex-linked rather than simply age/size-linked; recorded as a gap rather than asserted as a male-only trait.

similarSpecies.name: Yellowmouth grouper (Mycteroperca interstitialis)
similarSpecies.distinction: Yellowmouth grouper shows yellow coloration both inside and at the corners of the mouth; scamp shows yellow only at the mouth corners.

similarSpecies.name: Gag grouper
similarSpecies.distinction: Scamp has a more concave head profile, pronounced elongated soft dorsal/anal fin rays, and a body covered in sharply defined dark spots - gag lacks the spotted pattern and has a less concave profile.

identification.averageAdultLength: FWC describes common catches around 12 in, well below the documented maximum size below - a wide gap between the 'commonly caught' figure and the maximum that this record reports rather than resolves.
identification.commonAnglingSize: Legal fish must meet the 20 in TL South Atlantic minimum size where that rule applies; FWC's commonly-caught figure (about 12 in) is below that minimum and likely reflects undersized/released fish or a different regional dataset.
identification.typicalWeight: Not clearly sourced as distinct from the maximum-size figures below.
identification.maximumDocumentedSize: Up to about 43 in and 36 lb (SAFMC); FWC gives a maximum near 42 in, with the Florida state record standing at 28 lb 6 oz.
identification.longevity: May live up to about 30 years; the oldest documented age recorded was 21 years (SAFMC).
gaps: Whether the elongated fin-ray extensions are sex-linked (i.e., specific to transitioned males) or simply age/size-linked was not resolved by any source found.
No thermal preference or tolerance data (°F) was found for this species in any agency or peer-reviewed source searched; omitted from the catalog record entirely rather than guessed.
FWC's 'commonly caught around 12 in' figure and the 20 in South Atlantic minimum size are in tension and were not reconciled by any source found.

social.note: Described as a live-bottom resident that occasionally congregates over wrecks and rocky outcroppings rather than a schooling species; no source described adult social structure beyond that.

feedingStrategy.note: SAFMC describes scamp as aggressive predators that swallow crabs, shrimp, and other fish whole; FWC describes the diet as small fishes and invertebrates generally.

dielTendency.note: No agency or peer-reviewed source made a specific day/night feeding claim for this species; recorded as mixed rather than assigned confidently.

behavior.coverUse: Low-profile live bottom with dense soft coral and sponge growth is the preferred structure; wrecks and rocky outcroppings are used occasionally. Scamp are reported co-occurring on this live-bottom habitat with red grouper, white grunt, and red porgy.
behavior.spawningBehavior: Scamp are protogynous hermaphrodites, transitioning from female to male as they age. They spawn pelagic eggs offshore; SAFMC gives an April-May window, while FWC describes the timing more loosely as 'late spring.' As with other South Atlantic shallow-water grouper, harvest is closed during a defined spawning-season window as a conservation measure. This description is biological and regulatory context only - it does not identify, locate, or describe a spawning aggregation as a structure class to fish.
gaps: Spawning-window dates disagree between SAFMC (April-May) and FWC ('late spring'); recorded as a discrepancy rather than resolved.
No thermally-driven behavior, current-facing behavior, territoriality, cold-front response, or angling-pressure response was found in a usable source; all omitted rather than inferred.
No Gulf-specific behavioral detail was found separate from the South Atlantic-sourced material above.

diet.primaryNote: SAFMC describes scamp as aggressive predators that will swallow crabs, shrimp, and other fish whole; FWC describes the diet more generally as small fishes and invertebrates. Diet capacity is not evidence of a current feeding event.
diet.observedForageRule: Diet capacity is not proof that a feeding event is happening now. Observed current forage still comes from a user observation or Hatch Match, never from this record alone.
gaps: No life-stage, seasonal, or ontogenetic diet detail was found beyond the general adult prey list above.
Whether squid/cephalopods (mollusks class) feature in scamp diet, as they do for the closely related gag, was not specifically sourced for scamp and is omitted rather than assumed.

seasonal_calendar.overview: Scamp behavior in the sources reviewed centers on year-round live-bottom residency at 75-300 ft, with a spring offshore spawning-aggregation period that the South Atlantic manages with a harvest closure. This record limits itself to the reviewed nearshore/offshore structure classes outside that closure.
